title: Data Structures
objectives: Pick a structure by its dominant operation
Explain how a hash table achieves O(1) average
Know when trees, heaps and tries win

sections.markdown: A data structure organizes data so specific operations (insert, search, delete, traverse) are efficient. Choosing the right one often decides pass vs fail.

sections.code:
Hash table:
  index = hash(key) % capacity
  collisions -> chaining (list per bucket) or open addressing
  high load factor -> resize & rehash (keeps O(1) average)

sections.markdown: Hash tables are the most-used structure in interviews — they turn many O(n²) brute forces into O(n). When you think 'have I seen this?' or 'count occurrences', reach for a map/set.
Using a linked list when you need random access, or an array when you do many middle insertions. Match the structure to the dominant operation, not habit.

flashcards.front: How does a hash table get O(1)?
flashcards.back: It maps a key to a bucket via a hash; collisions are chained or probed, and it resizes to keep the load factor low.
Array: O(1) index, cache-friendly. Linked list: O(1) insert at ends, O(n) access.
Prefix queries — autocomplete, spell-check — keyed by characters.
When you repeatedly need the min/max — priority queues, Dijkstra, top-k.

quiz.explain: Hash tables give O(1) average lookup; arrays/lists are O(n) for search.

quiz.q: A balanced BST keeps operations at…
quiz.explain: Balancing (AVL/Red-Black) keeps height ~log n, so search/insert/delete are O(log n).
A trie is keyed by characters, making prefix search natural.

quiz.q: Arrays beat linked lists in practice mainly due to…
quiz.explain: Contiguous storage gives spatial locality, so the CPU cache helps.

challenges.text: Two Sum using a hash map in O(n).
